row_description: I am mocked as weird or poor or fat. It is unfair and not my fault. Wise: protect my self-respect, find spaces where I fit, and report harassment. Harmful: believing their story.
recipe_text: A letter or an email written by the protagonist to someone, in a natural voice.

record.passage:
Dear Rajni Masi,

You asked why I have gone quiet on the phone. The truth is that some kids in my class call me weird, poor, and other things about my body. They do it when the teacher isn't looking, and sometimes they copy how I talk. Last week someone stuck a note on my bag. I cried in the washroom and hated myself for a while. But I have been thinking: nothing they say is my fault. Their words are about them. I've started spending lunch in the art room, where nobody cares what I wear. Yesterday I showed the note to my class teacher, and she said she would deal with it. I wanted you to know, because I'm not alone in this.

Love,
Jasleen

qa.q: Where has Jasleen started spending lunch?
qa.a: In the art room.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel at first, and how has her thinking changed?
qa.a: She cried in the washroom and hated herself for a while, but now she believes the mocking is not her fault and that their words are about them.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do that helps her in this situation?
qa.a: She protected her self-respect by not believing their story, found a place where she fits in the art room, and reported the harassment by showing the note to her teacher.

qa.q: How might Rajni Masi feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably sad and protective, but also proud that Jasleen spoke up. She asked why Jasleen had gone quiet, so she cares and will be glad to know.

record.grounding: The protagonist is mocked, refuses to believe the story, finds a place to fit in and reports the harassment.

row_description: I go along with mean things because I fear being kicked out of the group. Belonging built on fear is fragile. Wise: quietly refuse one thing and see who still stands by me.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage:
"Just say it, Indu," Payal whispered at the lunch benches. "Say Rani smells funny."
"But she doesn't."
"Then you can sit somewhere else."
Indu's hands went cold. She laughed a small laugh that she did not mean, and Rani looked at her food.
"That was not funny," Indu said later, at the tap. "I'm sorry, Rani."
"Why did you do it?"
"I was scared they'd throw me out."
Next day Payal handed her a note to pass around. Indu quietly put it back in Payal's bag and said, "I'm not doing this one." Two girls, Meena and Sonal, shrugged and sat down next to her.

qa.q: Who did Payal want Indu to say smelled funny?
qa.a: Payal wanted Indu to say that Rani smells funny.

qa.q: Why did Indu laugh at first even though she did not mean it?
qa.a: She was scared of being thrown out of the group, so she went along with the mean joke.

qa.q: What small step did Indu take that showed who her real friends were?
qa.a: She refused just one thing, passing the note, and saw that Meena and Sonal still sat down with her.

qa.q: What might Rani have felt when Indu apologised at the tap?
qa.a: Rani may have felt hurt but also a little relieved that Indu admitted she was wrong, though she asked why it happened.

record.grounding: A child goes along with mean things out of fear of being expelled, then quietly refuses one thing and sees who stands by her.

row_description: I have seen bad police behaviour and I now see every uniform as a threat. Wise: stay careful without hating everyone, and know that many officers do their duty properly.
recipe_text: A letter or an email written by the protagonist to someone, in a natural voice.

record.passage:
Dear Damini,
You asked why I crossed the road yesterday when the constable was standing at the corner. Honest answer: since I saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near our market last month, every uniform feels like a warning. I tense up before anyone has done anything. But yesterday I watched that same constable for a while. He walked a lost old woman to the bus stand and held the traffic for her. That doesn't cancel what I saw, and I'll still be careful. But I don't want to treat everyone as a threat when some are doing their job properly. I'm still working it out. Tell me what you think.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir see an officer do last month?
qa.a: Tanvir saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near the market.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about uniforms, and how is that feeling shifting?
qa.a: Tanvir tenses up at every uniform as if it were a warning, but seeing the constable help a lost old woman makes Tanvir unwilling to treat everyone as a threat.

qa.q: How can Tanvir stay careful without hating everyone?
qa.a: By judging each officer by what they actually do, staying alert and polite, and remembering that one bad moment is not every officer.

qa.q: How might Damini feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and thoughtful, since Tanvir shares a hard feeling openly and asks what Damini thinks.

record.grounding: After seeing bad police behaviour Tanvir sees every uniform as a threat, then starts to stay careful without hating everyone.

row_description: All my friends have the new branded shoes and I feel left out. Wanting to fit in is human. I can ask myself whether friendship depends on shoes, and talk to my parents honestly.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage: I'm Akash, and I sit behind Aparna in class, so I noticed. On Monday six kids came in wearing the same new white shoes and lined up their feet for a photo. Aparna's shoes were old, with a patched heel. She laughed along but kept her feet under the desk. At break she didn't join them; she said she had to finish a drawing. On Thursday at the gate she told me, "I said to my mum that I want them, and I said I felt left out. She said we'll talk on Sunday." She sounded lighter, I think. I don't really know what she feels. She still plays with everybody.

qa.q: How many kids came in wearing the same new white shoes?
qa.a: Six kids did.

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling when she kept her feet under the desk?
qa.a: Possibly embarrassed or left out, though Akash cannot be sure from that alone.

qa.q: What step did Aparna take that could ease things at home?
qa.a: She told her mum honestly that she wanted the shoes and felt left out, and they planned to talk on Sunday.

qa.q: How does Akash see Aparna's situation?
qa.a: He notices her behaviour and that she seemed lighter later, but admits he does not know for sure what she feels.

record.grounding: A child feels left out over branded shoes and talks honestly to a parent, seen through a classmate's account.

row_description: A doctor who explains options honestly earns your trust. Share full information, follow the plan, and ask if you do not understand. Trust is not blind: you are a partner in your treatment.
recipe_text: A letter or an email written by the protagonist to someone, in a natural voice.

record.passage:
Dear Pradeep,
You asked how the appointment went. Dr Rao sat down, put her pen away, and explained the two options I have, including what each can and can't do and what she doesn't know yet. I admitted I'd missed some doses because the side effects scared me, and she didn't scold me; she changed how we'll manage it. When she used a word I didn't understand, I said so, and she drew a small diagram. I'll follow the plan, and I'll keep asking. I'm not handing my body over blindly; I'm part of the team. I felt steadier walking out than I have in weeks. Thank you for asking me to write it down instead of bottling it up.
Siddharth

qa.q: What did Dr Rao draw when Siddharth did not understand a word?
qa.a: Dr Rao drew a small diagram.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth admit having missed some doses?
qa.a: The side effects had scared Siddharth, and Dr Rao's honest, unhurried manner made it feel safe to share the full picture.

qa.q: What should Siddharth do if a later instruction is unclear?
qa.a: Say so and ask again, as before, keep following the plan and keep sharing full information with the doctor.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao have seen Siddharth's honesty about the doses?
qa.a: Probably as helpful, because it let the plan be adjusted to what was really happening.

record.grounding: A doctor who explains options honestly earns trust; sharing full information, following the plan and asking when unsure, as a partner in treatment.

row_description: The wrongdoer is a friend who helped me settle in, and I feel torn. Wise: loyalty to a person and loyalty to truth can clash; give him a chance to correct it, but do not stay silent forever. Harmful: excuses.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: The dairy society office in the kasba smelled of milk cans and damp registers. Jyoti had been there four months, and Farooq had been kind since the first week. He had found her a room and shown her the shortcut to the bus stand. So when she saw him shaving a little off the weights in the morning register, she stared at the page for a long time. Her chest felt tight. That evening she waited by the tea stall. "Farooq bhai, the entries don't match the scale. You need to fix them." He laughed, then looked away. "Everyone does it, it's small." "It's not small if it's the farmers' milk," she said, her voice shaking. "You have until Friday. After that I will have to tell the secretary." He said nothing, and she walked home wondering if she'd lost a friend.

qa.q: How long had Jyoti been at the dairy society office?
qa.a: Jyoti had been there four months.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she saw Farooq shaving the weights?
qa.a: Torn and tense: her chest felt tight, she stared at the page a long time, and she wondered if she had lost a friend.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that balanced loyalty and honesty?
qa.a: She spoke to Farooq privately, asked him to fix the entries by Friday and said she would tell the secretary afterwards.

qa.q: How might Farooq have felt hearing Jyoti's words at the tea stall?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and defensive, since he laughed, looked away and said everyone does it.

record.grounding: The wrongdoer is a friend who helped her settle in; she feels torn, gives him a chance to correct it, and sets a limit on silence.

row_description: A landlord refuses to rent to me because of who I am. I feel angry and small. Wise: it says more about his prejudice; know the legal options, keep notes, find allies and other options. Harmful: internalising it.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative with a complication or constraint added (time pressure, little money, a noisy place, a missing person, bad weather), still faithful to the row.

record.passage: With the hostel closing in three days and monsoon rain flooding the road, Afreen stood under a shop awning while the broker held out his phone. "Jagdish-ji says no. He won't rent to your community. Sorry." He shrugged as if it were about the weather. Afreen's face burned. She was angry and, underneath, small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself. Then she reminded herself that a refusal like this shows what the landlord believes, not what she is. She opened her notes app and typed the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name. She rang Sana from the college legal aid clinic, who offered to explain her options. That evening Afreen's classmate said her cousin had a room going, and Afreen went to see it in the rain.

qa.q: How many days were left before the hostel closed?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel beneath her anger after the refusal?
qa.a: She felt small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that turned the refusal into action?
qa.a: She noted the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name, contacted the legal aid clinic and followed a lead on another room.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see his refusal?
qa.a: He may see it as an ordinary decision about his property, though it rests on a prejudice that reflects on him, not on Afreen.

record.grounding: A landlord refuses her because of who she is; she feels angry and small, keeps notes, seeks legal aid and allies, and finds another option.

row_description: I have cut contact with a parent after long pain and feel relief mixed with grief. The choice can be necessary for safety and peace; I check that I am acting from clarity and not from anger, and leave the door open only if it is safe.
recipe_text: A letter or an email written by the protagonist to someone, in a natural voice.

record.passage:
Dear Joseph,

You asked why I did not come to Diwali dinner, so I will tell you plainly. Three months ago I stopped answering my father's calls. There were years of shouting and cutting remarks, and after my brother's wedding it got worse. The first week I felt lighter and slept through the night. In the second week I cried in the supermarket over a packet of his favourite biscuits. I keep asking myself whether I am punishing him. I do not think so. I think I am protecting myself. Still, I have written a note to myself: if he ever changes, and when I know I am safe, I will listen. For now I am keeping the door on the latch.

Love,
Anjali

qa.q: How long ago did Anjali stop answering the father's calls?
qa.a: Anjali stopped answering three months ago.

qa.q: What does Anjali's crying in the supermarket suggest?
qa.a: The relief is mixed with grief, and Anjali still misses something about the father.

qa.q: How can Anjali check that this comes from clarity and not anger?
qa.a: By asking whether the aim is protecting oneself rather than punishing, as Anjali does, and keeping the door ajar only where safety allows.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have asked about the missed dinner?
qa.a: Joseph noticed Anjali's absence and probably cares and is puzzled or worried.

record.grounding: The writer has cut contact with a father after long pain, feels relief mixed with grief, checks the motive and leaves the door only latched.

row_description: A friend congratulates you but seems sour, or teases you about your new status. Stay humble, avoid showing off, and keep the friendship anchored in shared history. Give them space, and share their wins too.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage:
"Congratulations, sir," Ramesh said, bowing. "Manager Jatin. Will you still eat at the roadside stall with us poor people?"

Jatin laughed but felt the edge. "Stop it. I'm still the guy who owes you forty rupees from class ten."

"Forty-five, with interest."

"Fine. Chai's on me tonight, and you choose the place."

Ramesh shrugged. "I heard they gave you a car allowance too."

"Just the title, honestly. I got lucky that the other manager left." Jatin paused. "How did the interview go? You said you had one last week."

"They said they'd call."

"Call me before you go in next time. I'll drill you on the tough questions, like you did for my board practicals."

Ramesh looked away, then smiled. "Fine. Bring the notes."

qa.q: How much does Jatin say he owes Ramesh from class ten?
qa.a: Jatin says he owes forty rupees, which Ramesh corrects to forty-five with interest.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's "poor people" line suggest about how Ramesh feels?
qa.a: It suggests a sour mix of envy and hurt at Jatin's new status, hidden behind teasing.

qa.q: How does Jatin keep the friendship steady?
qa.a: Jatin stays humble by playing down the promotion, brings up shared history, and offers to pay for chai and help Ramesh prepare for the interview.

qa.q: Why might Ramesh have looked away before smiling?
qa.a: Ramesh may have felt stung about the job hunt while still being touched by Jatin's offer of help.

record.grounding: A friend congratulates Jatin with a sour edge; Jatin stays humble, anchors in shared history, gives space and offers to help with the friend's own goal.

row_description: A close friend has stopped replying and I feel dropped and puzzled. I reach out once directly, without blame, and accept the answer, including silence; I avoid rewriting the whole friendship as fake.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage:
For three weeks Baljeet's messages had stopped, and Lokesh checked his phone at the chai stall each morning. The tea maker noticed and said nothing. Lokesh felt dropped, and puzzled. One night on the roof he caught himself thinking, It was all fake, after the cricket tournaments and the bus rides to the mela. He knew that wasn't true.

He typed one message: "I miss talking to you. Did I do something? Whatever the answer, I'd rather know than guess." Then he put the phone in his pocket.

Days passed with no reply. At the mela Lokesh ate jalebi alone and remembered Baljeet dragging him onto the big wheel when he was afraid. That memory was real, and stayed real. He decided to leave the door open and stop checking.

qa.q: What did Lokesh write in his one message?
qa.a: He asked whether he had done something and said he would rather know than guess.

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel when Baljeet stopped replying?
qa.a: Dropped and puzzled; he even caught himself thinking it was all fake.

qa.q: What helped Lokesh cope with the silence?
qa.a: He sent one direct message without blame, kept the true memories, and stopped checking his phone while leaving the door open.

qa.q: What might be going on for Baljeet?
qa.a: The passage doesn't say; Baljeet's silence could have many reasons, and Lokesh accepts not knowing rather than assuming the worst.

record.grounding: A close friend stops replying; Lokesh reaches out once without blame, accepts silence and does not rewrite the friendship as fake.

row_description: Calls from loan apps or recovery agents make you anxious. Know that harassment is illegal, keep records, talk to the bank about restructuring, and avoid borrowing from a new app to repay an old one.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage:
Irawati's phone buzzed for the fourth time before lunch: an unknown number, the loan app's recovery team. Her stomach tightened. "Pay today or we will message your contacts," said the latest voicemail.

In the office pantry she whispered to her colleague Asif, "I keep thinking of taking a loan from a different app to clear this one."

"Don't," Asif said. "That's how it stacks up." He suggested she save every call log and voicemail, note the times, and go to her bank about a repayment plan. "And threats like that are harassment, Irawati. It can be reported."

She opened a notes file and began listing the date, the number and what was said. Her hands slowed. She would ask the bank for an appointment first thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the latest voicemail threaten?
qa.a: It said that if she did not pay today they would message her contacts.

qa.q: What was Irawati tempted to do, and what does it show about her state?
qa.a: She was tempted to take a loan from a different app to clear this one, which shows how anxious and cornered she felt.

qa.q: What should Irawati do next?
qa.a: Save the call logs and voicemails, note dates and times, talk to the bank about a repayment plan, and report the harassment.

qa.q: How does Asif see the idea of a second loan?
qa.a: Asif sees it as a trap, since that is how debt stacks up.

record.grounding: Calls from a loan app's recovery team make Irawati anxious; a colleague steers her to keep records, talk to the bank and avoid a new loan.

row_description: The feed keeps serving more of what upsets or hooks me, and hours vanish. Recognise it: apps are designed for attention. Wise: set limits, curate follows, and step away.
recipe_text: Before / during / after across a few days or weeks, in three short beats showing change over time; each beat happens on a different day.

record.passage:
Tuesday: Devika opened the app for one quick look at a cooking clip. Ninety minutes later she was still there, watching strangers shout at each other, each video angrier than the last, her jaw tight. Her homework sat untouched.
Friday: Manjula noticed her friend's puffy eyes. "You keep saying the app knows what you like. I think it knows what keeps you." Devika frowned, then admitted that whenever she paused on an upsetting clip, more of them came.
The next Wednesday: Devika set a daily limit, unfollowed the angry pages and followed two pottery makers. When the reminder buzzed, she put the phone in a drawer and helped her mother chop onions.

qa.q: What did Devika follow after she unfollowed the angry pages?
qa.a: She followed two pottery makers.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as the clips got angrier, and what tells you?
qa.a: She was getting tense and upset, shown by her tight jaw, yet she kept watching because each clip pulled her to the next.

qa.q: Why do Devika's steps suit an app built to hold attention?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit, curating what she follows and stepping away when the reminder buzzed all cut down how much the feed can keep serving her.

qa.q: How might Manjula have seen the change in Devika?
qa.a: Manjula noticed the puffy eyes and explained gently, so probably felt worried at first and relieved to see Devika take control.

record.grounding: Shows a teen recognising a feed designed for attention and setting limits and curating follows.

row_description: Countdown timers, "only 5 seats" and screenshots of profits push me to hurry. Wise: urgency is a sales tool; slow down, read the risks, and never invest money I cannot afford to lose.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage:
The village cyber shop had one working fan, and Pranav sat under it staring at a group message: a countdown clock, "ONLY 5 SEATS LEFT", and screenshots of strangers' profits. The clock had eleven minutes on it. His savings from the harvest season were in the phone wallet.

His heart was racing. Everyone in the group seemed to be saying "joined!"

His sister Vidya, home for the weekend, glanced at the screen. "Why is the timer red?"

"So I don't miss it."

"Or so you don't think." She scrolled up. "Where are the risks written? Everything here is screenshots."

Pranav looked at the clock again. Then he closed the group, put the phone face down, and said, "Let's read the fine print first, didi."

qa.q: How many seats did the message say were left?
qa.a: The message said "ONLY 5 SEATS LEFT".

qa.q: Why was Pranav's heart racing?
qa.a: The countdown clock and the messages saying "joined!" made Pranav fear he would miss out, so he felt pushed to hurry with his harvest savings.

qa.q: What would you advise Pranav to do before putting money in?
qa.a: Slow down, read the risks in writing, treat the countdown as a sales tool, and only ever use money he could afford to lose.

qa.q: How does Vidya see the red timer differently from Pranav?
qa.a: Vidya sees the timer as pressure meant to stop people thinking, while Pranav sees it as a real deadline, which is why she asks where the risks are written.

record.grounding: Countdown timers, limited seats and profit screenshots pressure Pranav to hurry until his sister helps him slow down and look for the risks.

row_description: A manager gave you a chance when others did not. Feel the gratitude, but also stay honest. Thanks does not mean silence when you see an error; a good manager will value your candid input.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.passage: Three interviews had ended with the same polite line about my missing experience. Then Bhupen read my portfolio and said, "Start on the fifteenth." I have never forgotten that. So when I found that the pricing sheet Bhupen had sent to two clients used the old tax rate, my chest went tight. It felt ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who took a chance on me. I waited a day. Then I walked over with the sheet in hand and said, "I think this rate is outdated. Could we check?" Bhupen looked, groaned, and said, "Thank you. Send me the corrected version and I will call both clients." I understood then that being honest was one of the ways of saying thanks. Sabina

qa.q: What was wrong with the pricing sheet Bhupen sent to two clients?
qa.a: It used the old tax rate.

qa.q: Why did Sabina wait a day before speaking up?
qa.a: Sabina felt it would be ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who had taken a chance on Sabina.

qa.q: What made Sabina's way of raising the error work well?
qa.a: Sabina brought the sheet and asked whether the rate could be checked, so Bhupen could fix it quickly without feeling blamed.

qa.q: How did Bhupen react to the correction?
qa.a: Bhupen thanked Sabina and planned to call both clients, which shows candid input was welcome.

record.grounding: The narrator, grateful to a manager who gave a chance, still points out an error, showing thanks and honesty can go together.

row_description: Seeing an insulting pile-on against someone, you feel righteous and jump in. Pause: do you know the full story, and would you say it in person? Mobs do real harm; challenge wrongdoing with facts and proportion.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage: Eshaan here. My flatmate Chinmay was on the sofa, jaw set, thumbs flying, when I brought tea. A clip was going around of a shopkeeper shouting at a customer, and hundreds of people were tearing into him in the replies. Chinmay had a draft open: three lines, each nastier than the last. He looked ready to post. Then he stopped, scrolled up, and searched for the longer video. I saw him watch it twice. "The start is cut off," he said, mostly to himself. "The customer was pushing him." He deleted the draft and wrote one line asking people to wait for the whole clip. Whether he felt embarrassed or just calmer, I couldn't say. He drank the cold tea and put the phone down.

qa.q: What was going around online that had Chinmay typing?
qa.a: A clip of a shopkeeper shouting at a customer was going around.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have stopped and searched for the longer video?
qa.a: He seems to have started wondering whether he knew the full story. Eshaan cannot say if he then felt embarrassed or simply calmer.

qa.q: How could Chinmay challenge behaviour he thinks is wrong without joining a pile-on?
qa.a: Check the whole story first, use facts and stay proportionate, as with the single line asking people to wait for the whole clip. Asking whether he would say it in person also helps.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper have experienced the hundreds of replies?
qa.a: Probably as frightening and hurtful, being torn into by strangers over a clip with the start cut off. A request to wait for the whole clip might come as a relief.

record.grounding: Righteous anger at a pile-on: pausing to check the full story before joining, and choosing a proportionate, factual response instead.

row_description: I was unfaithful and I am torn between shame, self-justification, and fear of being found out. The honest path is to face what I did and the harm it caused; the harmful path is hiding, blaming my partner, or asking them to soothe me.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.passage: You asked why I'm so strict about honesty, so listen. I'm Minakshi, and at twenty-four I was unfaithful to my partner Bhavna. I told myself Bhavna had been distant, that it was only once, that no one would ever know. Mostly I felt sick, afraid that someone would discover it, and under that, ashamed. One night Bhavna asked, "Is something wrong?" and the easy lie was right there in my mouth. I put the cup down and said, "Yes. I did something that hurt you, and I'm going to tell you." I didn't say it was Bhavna's fault. I didn't ask to be comforted. Bhavna cried and went to a sister's house for a week, and I had no right to ask for anything. Hiding would have been so much easier, and so much worse.

qa.q: How old was Minakshi when the unfaithfulness happened?
qa.a: Minakshi was twenty-four.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling underneath the excuses?
qa.a: Fear of discovery, and under that, shame. Minakshi felt sick, and the excuses were a way of holding those feelings off.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that faced the harm, and what would have made it worse?
qa.a: Minakshi told Bhavna the truth without blaming Bhavna or asking for comfort. Continuing to hide, or excusing it as Bhavna's distance, would have made it worse.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt hearing Minakshi's confession?
qa.a: Hurt and overwhelmed, since Bhavna cried and went to a sister's house for a week. Being told honestly, rather than discovering it, may still have mattered.

record.grounding: Shows someone who was unfaithful, torn between shame, self-justification and fear of discovery, choosing to face what they did without blaming the partner or asking to be soothed.

row_description: I start believing this preacher has all the answers and see others as lost. Harmful: a single voice takes over my thinking. Wise: stay curious, keep diverse friends, and check claims.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: On the bus to the kasba school, Nirmala played the preacher's talk on one earphone and ignored the chatter. "He says most people are lost," Nirmala told Tenzin. "He has the answer to everything." Tenzin raised an eyebrow. "Everything?" At the momo stall after school, a thought arrived: Tenzin was lost, and so were the two girls at the next table. Nirmala noticed how the thought felt: cold. That night Nirmala searched for the figure the preacher had quoted about villages and found a different number from the district office. Nirmala frowned and saved a note: ask Tenzin's aunt, the teacher. On Saturday Nirmala went to Tenzin's mother's shop as usual.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala listen to the preacher's talk?
qa.a: Nirmala listened on the bus to the kasba school, with one earphone.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel on noticing the thought that Tenzin was lost?

Then he ran three laps around the kabaddi ground until his lungs burned. Afterwards he sat by his friend Bhola and said, "I'm so angry I could scream." Bhola just said, "Okay. Tell me."

record.passage:

record.passage:
In the Monday meeting at a Melbourne design studio, Diego sat at the far end with a closed notebook while everyone else argued about the timeline. Layla noticed the silence again: eyes down, chair pushed back. She wondered if it was fear of her.

row_description: A friend asks for a loan again. Wise: help within your means as a gift, be honest about your limit, and do not lend what strains you. Harmful: silent resentment or lying that you have none.

record.passage:
Zeenat's message came in while I was doing laundry. "Can you spare some for the mess bill again? Will return, promise." My name is Tanuja, and that word "again" sat in my stomach. Last time she promised too. I hadn't minded the money as much as the pretending: I'd smiled at her, then complained about her to my roommate.

This time I sat on my bunk and worked out what I could give without skipping my own bus pass. I wrote back, "I can give a small amount, and please treat it as a gift, not a loan. That's my limit for now."

She sent a heart, and later, "thanks for being straight." I felt lighter, though a bit anxious that she might feel judged. I still don't know if she'll ask again.

qa.a: Possibly embarrassed or judged at first. Her heart and "thanks for being straight" suggest relief at an honest answer.

record.grounding: A friend asks for a loan again; Tanuja gives within her means as a gift and states her limit honestly.

row_description: I miss home food, language and family and cry in secret. Wise: schedule calls, cook familiar meals, find fellow migrants, and know that it eases with time. Harmful: isolating or judging myself for missing home.

She helped him find dried chillies at the market and they cooked a big pot of beans. record.passage:
"Kashish, let me tell you why I frowned at the message you showed me," said Avni. "When I was twenty-four, a stranger in a chat offered me an easy work-from-home job: rate videos, earn a fixed amount for each one. All I had to do was pay a small deposit to activate my account. "Then I got greedy. They said bigger deposits paid more, so I put in more. The account froze, and the stranger vanished. Only afterwards did I ask the question I should have asked first: why would anyone give away money for clicking? I never checked whether the company was registered.

qa.a: Ask why a stranger would give money away, check whether the company is registered, and never pay in order to earn.

qa.a: As a hopeful person who could be drawn in with a small payout and then pushed to deposit more.

record.grounding: An easy remote-job offer works on Avni's hope and greed; Avni is left with the lesson to ask why a stranger would give money away and never pay to earn.

He listed the problems: the crowded station, the ticket checker, her phone battery. She laughed a little, then didn't. "You said the same before I went to hostel. I lived."

Imran wanted to shout, "Because I called you every night." He swallowed it. "Take my power bank. Message me when you board and when you arrive. Take the ladies' coach if it feels better. But you decide."

"That I can do," Parveen said.

At the platform he handed her a packet of biscuits, not another warning. When the train pulled out, his hands were shaking, and he let them.

qa.a: Anxious. He gripped the seat, listed one problem after another and wanted to shout.

record.grounding: Imran wants to shield his younger sister from mistakes and, under time pressure, gives guidance while letting her decide.

record.passage:

row_description: Their exes bother you more than they should. Wise: accept the past is not a threat and talk about the fear itself. Immature: interrogating details or bringing it up as a weapon in arguments.
recipe_text: An interview-style or spoken monologue: the protagonist tells the story aloud to a friend, podcast host or interviewer.

record.passage:
Charu, promise you won't laugh. Me, Rekha, the sensible one, and I've been jealous of Ishaan's exes.

He mentioned a girl from school once, just once, and I couldn't stop. I asked what they used to do on Sundays, whether he'd loved her more than me, how long they had kept texting. He answered honestly at first, and then he got tired of it. And in our last argument, I actually said, "Well, you'd have gone to her party, wouldn't you?" like a weapon.

I saw his face fall. Later, on my own, I realised the questions weren't about her at all. I was scared I'd never be as interesting as anyone before me.

So I told him that: "It's my fear, not a charge against you." He looked so relieved. We haven't talked about her since, and I don't need to.

Sunday night.

Third path this year. First a yoga class, then a breathing workshop, and today a talk by a visiting teacher who said enlightenment could be had in one weekend for a fee. My burnout hasn't lifted since March, and I wanted it to be true.

Indu, sitting beside me, whispered, "A weekend? For that price?" and I laughed out loud with relief. I'm not signing up.

I want to go slowly. Ten minutes of sitting each morning for a month, then see whether I'm less snappy at work and whether I sleep better. If a teaching can't survive a Tuesday at the office, it isn't much use. And I want to ask more questions, not fewer.

Seeking isn't silly. It's just me trying to find my way out of a fog.

Vaibhav

qa.a: With suspicion about both the promise and the price, as "A weekend? For that price?" shows.

Parveen

row_description: A younger person keeps making mistakes you once made. Remember your own learning curve, explain reasons rather than orders, and let them try safe failures. Mentoring is investing, not proving superiority.

record.passage: The third time Ishita sent a client email without the attachment, I felt my jaw tighten. Then I remembered my own first month, when I sent a quote to the wrong client and hid in the pantry. So I didn't say "again?" I said, "Let's make a checklist together, and you tell me what could go wrong." I explained why the attachment matters: the client reads it first, and an email without it looks careless even when it isn't. The next week Ishita caught it half a second before pressing send and grinned at me across the desk. I'm Aditi, three years senior. Not a genius, just someone who already made those mistakes.

row_description: I let out a secret in a fight and now feel awful. Honesty is best: say sorry, no excuses, and accept that trust may take time. Blaming her for making me angry hides my responsibility.
recipe_text: Before / during / after across a few days or weeks, in three short beats showing change over time; each beat happens on a different day.

record.passage:
Monday. During a quarrel over the cricket score, Vijay shouted, "At least I don't cry in the toilets when I miss the choir!" Sarita's mouth fell open. The whole line of children heard.

Thursday. He found Sarita by the water tank. "I'm sorry I told everyone your secret. It was mine to keep, and I broke it. No excuses." Sarita looked at her shoes. "I'm still upset," she said. "I don't know when I'll feel okay." Vijay nodded. "That's fair. I'll wait."

qa.a: He shouted, "At least I don't cry in the toilets when I miss the choir!"

qa.a: She is probably still hurt and embarrassed because the whole line heard, so she needs time even though the sorry was honest.

record.grounding: A child lets out a friend's secret in a fight, feels awful, apologises without excuses and accepts that trust may take time.

row_description: An older cousin who works in the field tells me honestly the good and bad of a career. I trust the honesty more than the glamour. Wise: hear more than one voice before deciding.

record.passage: Sumit had watched three videos about architecture, all glossy buildings and sunsets, and none had made him trust anything. So during the Diwali visit he cornered Urmila didi on the balcony. "Is it really as cool as it looks?" Urmila laughed. "Honestly? The studies are long, clients change their minds at the last minute, and I've missed family dinners. But when a house I drew has people living in it, that's a good feeling." row_description: I learn to say "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect". Wise: self-compassion makes accountability easier, not weaker. Harmful: using kindness to excuse repeating the harm.
recipe_text: Before / during / after across a few days or weeks, in three short beats showing change over time; each beat happens on a different day.

record.passage:
Monday. Ramesh forgot to return Yamini's notes before her exam, and she had to borrow a classmate's at the last minute. "I'm useless," he told the ceiling that night. The words felt heavy and no use to anyone.
Thursday. In the hostel washroom mirror he tried a different sentence, aloud: "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect." It felt odd. Then he went to find Yamini. "I was careless and it cost you. I'm sorry. Here are the notes and a set of my own copies." She nodded. "Thanks for saying it straight."
Two weeks later. Ramesh caught himself about to be late again with a borrowed book and set a phone reminder instead of just feeling bad about it.

qa.a: Probably relieved and respected, since she thanked him for saying it straight.

record.grounding: The protagonist learns to say he made a mistake and is still worth respect; self-compassion makes it easier to apologise, repair and change.

row_description: You went along once and now feel sick about it. Guilt is useful if it leads to repair: come clean where possible, correct the record, and refuse a second time. Wallowing or hiding deepens the harm.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage:
I'm Amandeep, and I share a desk row with Chandrika, so I've seen her this month. It began on the fifteenth, when she put her name to a delivery report that she knew had one wrong figure. She said afterwards it was her manager's idea. She didn't say it was fine.

For two weeks she stopped eating lunch with us. I noticed her rereading that report at her desk more than once, jaw tight. I can't say for sure what she was thinking.

Last Wednesday, she walked into her manager's office and stayed for twenty minutes. When she came out she told me quietly, "I've corrected the record and sent the client a note." A day later the manager asked her to sign off on another report with a similar figure. She said no.

She still looks tired. But she's eating lunch with us again.

qa.a: Chandrika signed it on the fifteenth.

qa.a: Chandrika corrected the record, sent the client a note, and refused to sign a second report with a similar figure.

row_description: I say fine, go play with her, but keep score of every time she chose others. Better to say the hurt out loud once, calmly. Silent resentment grows and slowly turns into cruelty.

record.passage:
Deepak said, "Fine, go play with Tara," and watched Mahima run to the colony park, where the new girl waited. He kicked a pebble. That was the third time this week she had picked someone else. He counted them like coins: Monday at lunch, Tuesday on the swings, now this.
He kept the list in his head all evening and felt hot every time he looked at it. A mean sentence about Tara rose to his tongue.
Instead, the next morning he said, quietly, "It hurt when you chose Tara at lunch. I just wanted you to know."
Mahima looked surprised. "Oh. I didn't think."

qa.q: How many times had Mahima picked someone else this week, by Deepak's count?
qa.a: Three times, counting Monday at lunch, Tuesday on the swings, and now.

qa.a: He could say calmly, once, that it hurt, as he did the next morning, rather than let the list grow.

qa.a: She probably had no idea, since she says she did not think, and only saw a friend saying fine.

record.grounding: A boy says 'fine' but silently counts every time his friend chose others, then says the hurt out loud once, calmly.

row_description: I stop reacting to comparisons and go numb, telling myself I do not care. Wise: check whether I truly stopped caring or just stopped feeling; then have one honest talk. Harmful: turning off effort altogether.

record.passage:
Sunday. At lunch Harsha's father said, "Your cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship. Take a lesson." Harsha kept chewing. "Okay." Inside, he told himself he didn't care.

Thursday. His maths homework sat unopened for three days. When his friend asked, he shrugged. "Why bother?" He noticed the flatness: no anger, no shame, just a grey nothing where those used to be.

The following Saturday. In the kitchen, he asked himself: Do I not care, or have I just stopped feeling it? He suspected the second. He told his mother Gargi, quietly, "I stopped listening when Papa compares me. I think it still hurts." She put the ladle down and said, "Then tell me what it feels like."

qa.a: He said his cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship.

qa.a: He suspected he hadn't stopped caring but had stopped feeling, because the hurt was still there under the grey nothing.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next to avoid shutting down his effort altogether?
qa.a: He can keep the honest talk with Gargi going and go back to his homework, since numbness protects him only in the short term.

qa.q: How might Harsha's mother see his shrug at first?
qa.a: Possibly as not caring, which is why hearing that it still hurts probably surprised her and made her put down the ladle.

record.grounding: Shows a teen who goes numb to comparisons and tells himself he does not care, then notices it and has one honest talk.

row_description: I beg my parents for something I saw in an ad and they refuse. I feel angry and it seems unfair. Understanding their limits and offering to save for it myself shows growing maturity.

row_description: You replay what you said wrong. Wise: notice the loop, talk to a friend, and give yourself the closure they did not. Harmful: blaming yourself.

record.grounding: A best friend shared a secret; Olga feels humiliated and enraged, says clearly what happened and lets the friendship's future depend on the repair.

Every month the same fight: I bought a nice lamp and Tenzin's jaw tightened; Tenzin saved every spare rupee and I felt I was being watched. I felt controlled. Tenzin felt I was careless. One night, tired, I asked instead of arguing: "What does being safe mean to you?" Tenzin went quiet, then said, "When I was small, we lost everything in one bad season." Something in me softened. I told Tenzin that safety for me meant not being afraid to enjoy a little. We sat with a notebook and made one budget together, with a fixed amount each that neither of us questioned. row_description: The teacher says my name sternly in front of the class. My face burns and I want to hide. Wise help is a quiet talk after and a chance to fix it. A harsh public telling-off can make a child feel bad instead of learning what to do.
recipe_text: A note written by an adult who watched: caregiver, teacher, counsellor, coach or supervisor (their observations, plus what they did next).

record.passage: Note from Sudha, class teacher. Today I said "Mohit!" sharply in front of everyone when he tore a page in the story book. His face went red, his chin dropped and he pulled his collar up to his ears. He did not speak for the rest of circle time. I realised my tone had made him want to hide. Afterwards I knelt at his desk and said quietly, "Books are for gentle hands. Shall we mend the page together?" He nodded and reached for the tape.

qa.q: What did Mohit tear in the story book?
qa.a: He tore a page.

qa.q: What did Mohit's red face and raised collar suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest shame and a wish to hide. His silence for the rest of circle time points the same way.

qa.q: What did Sudha change after seeing how Mohit reacted?
qa.a: She spoke to him quietly after class and offered a chance to fix the page together, instead of scolding in public.

qa.q: How might Mohit's classmates have seen the sharp call of his name?
qa.a: They probably felt tense and may have been afraid of being called out too. It can teach them to hide mistakes rather than to fix them.

record.grounding: The teacher says my name sternly in front of the class and my face burns; a quiet talk afterwards with a chance to fix it is wiser.

row_description: After a sincere apology I decide to trust them slowly with small things. Wise: watch consistent behaviour over words. Harmful: pretending nothing happened or demanding total forgiveness at once.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage:
"You read it, right? The apology?" Jeevan asked, leaning on the cycle shed wall.
"Twice."
"So are we okay?"
"Not all the way," Anirban said. "But I want to try. Here's something small. I'm nervous about the maths olympiad tryouts. Don't tell anyone."
"Not even Chinmay?"
"Not even him."
"I won't. Promise."
Anirban unlocked his cycle. "I'm not testing you. I'm just going to watch what happens."
"That's fair," Jeevan said quietly.
Two weeks later Anirban's phone buzzed.
Jeevan: Chinmay asked me about the olympiad today. I said ask Anirban yourself.
Anirban: Thanks 🙂
Anirban read it again at the bus stop. His shoulders dropped a little, and he decided that next week he might tell Jeevan something slightly bigger.

qa.q: What small thing did Anirban tell Jeevan at the cycle shed?
qa.a: He said he was nervous about the maths olympiad tryouts.

qa.q: What does Anirban mean by "I'm not testing you"?
qa.a: He wants to trust Jeevan slowly and is watching what Jeevan does rather than only what Jeevan says.

qa.q: What could Jeevan keep doing to rebuild the trust?
qa.a: Keep small promises, like keeping the olympiad secret, steadily over time, without asking for full forgiveness at once.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel hearing "Not all the way"?
qa.a: A little disappointed but relieved to have a chance. Jeevan answers "That's fair" and then keeps the promise.

record.grounding: After a sincere apology Anirban trusts Jeevan slowly with small things and watches Jeevan's consistent behaviour.

row_description: Offers a toy to keep the play going; feels the warmth of reciprocity when the friend shares back.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage: "Sunaina, do you want the red car?" "Yes! Are you sure?" "You can drive it to the garage. I'll be the mechanic." "Okay, thank you, Rajni." "Vroom, vroom, it's broken!" "I'll fix it with my spanner." A minute later: "Rajni, you want my blue truck?" "Can I? I'll carry the bricks." "Yes, we can work together." "This is fun, right?" "Yes, the best game!" 😊

qa.q: What did Rajni offer Sunaina?
qa.a: Rajni offered Sunaina the red car.

qa.q: Why did Rajni give Sunaina the car, and how did Rajni feel when Sunaina offered the truck?
qa.a: Rajni wanted the game to keep going, so Rajni gave it up and took the mechanic role. When Sunaina offered the truck back, Rajni was pleased and eager, asking "Can I?" and saying it was the best game. 😊

qa.q: What could the two friends do if both later want the same truck?
qa.a: They could remember how sharing worked before and take turns or find another job in the game.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after Rajni offers the car?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel welcomed and grateful, which makes Sunaina want to share the truck in return.

record.grounding: A child offers a toy to keep play going and feels the warmth of reciprocity when the friend shares back.

row_description: They say if you loved them you would. Wise: you decide your pace; someone who respects you accepts a no. Harmful: giving in out of fear of losing them. Talk to a trusted friend if pressure continues.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.passage: I am Anjali. Joseph and I had been together four months when he began saying it: "If you really loved me, you would." Sometimes he said it softly, sometimes as a joke, once with his jaw tight, outside my gate after a film. I kept apologising, and hated that I was apologising. That night I sat on my bed with a knot in my stomach, wondering whether he would leave. Next day I told my friend Rekha, who said, "Love that makes you scared to say no isn't a test you have to pass." So I told Joseph plainly that I set my own pace and that no meant no. He went quiet and said he needed to think. I still don't know how it will end. But for the first time in weeks I could breathe.

qa.q: How long had Anjali and Joseph been together when he began saying it?
qa.a: They had been together four months.

qa.q: What was Anjali afraid of on the night she sat on her bed?
qa.a: She was afraid Joseph would leave if she said no. The knot in her stomach and her constant apologising show fear and self-doubt.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if Joseph keeps pressuring her?
qa.a: She could keep saying no plainly, keep talking to Rekha or another trusted person, and remember that someone who respects her accepts a no.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Anjali's situation?
qa.a: Rekha sees a friend being made to feel scared, and points out that love should not make someone afraid to say no.

record.grounding: A partner says 'if you loved me you would', and the protagonist decides her own pace and talks to a trusted friend.

row_description: Juniors or friends treat you as perfect. Wise: stay honest about flaws and do not let it inflate you. Harmful: using their admiration.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative with a complication or constraint added (time pressure, little money, a noisy place, a missing person, bad weather), still faithful to the row.

record.passage: The corridor outside the viva room was loud with first-years, and Vijay had ten minutes to spare when Sarita caught his sleeve. "Vijay bhaiya, you never fail at anything! How do you do it?" Two other juniors leaned in, waiting. He could feel how nice it would be to just nod. Instead he laughed and said, "I failed two papers in my first year. I nearly quit. I sat in the library for a whole month with a friend who explained things to me." Sarita blinked. "Really?" "Really. Don't put me on a shelf, I fall off it." He glanced at the clock, waved, and went in for his viva, a little nervous, and glad he had said it.

qa.q: What did Sarita ask Vijay in the corridor?
qa.a: She asked how he never failed at anything.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel as the juniors leaned in, and what did he decide?
qa.a: He felt how nice it would be to just nod and be admired, but he chose to be honest about his failures instead.

qa.q: What could Vijay do to keep the juniors' admiration healthy?
qa.a: He can keep sharing honest stories about setbacks and what helped him, and avoid using their admiration to get favours.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Vijay after his answer?
qa.a: Sarita may be surprised but also encouraged, since she learns that even someone she looks up to failed and recovered. Her "Really?" shows her picture of him shifting.

record.grounding: Juniors treat the protagonist as perfect; he stays honest about his flaws and does not let it inflate him.

row_description: I blame the system, quotas, connections and English accents, and there may be some truth in it. Wise: name what is unfair without letting it become the whole story, then control what I can. Harmful: bitterness that stops effort.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage: I'm Alka. Bhupen and I were in the same batch, and lately his talk is all about how the process is rigged: referrals, polished English accents, seats that go by quota. I know some of it is true. Last month a panel asked where he learned his English, in a tone he did not like. But this week his laptop has stayed shut. Yesterday I mentioned two clerk openings and he said, "What's the point." Today, though, I found him in the library with a spoken English book, muttering the lines under his breath, and he sighed and said, "Unfair, yes. But I still need the job." Then he opened the form. I can't tell if he's bitter or planning. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did the panel ask Bhupen last month?
qa.a: The panel asked where he learned his English.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be feeling when he says "What's the point"?
qa.a: He may feel discouraged and bitter, though Alka says she can't tell for sure what is in his mind.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do with the parts of the process that really are unfair?
qa.a: He could name them honestly, then put effort into what he can control, like the spoken English practice and sending the applications.

qa.q: How does Alka see Bhupen's complaints?
qa.a: Alka accepts that some of it is true but worries the anger may stop his effort, and admits she can't tell if he is bitter or planning.

record.grounding: Bhupen blames the system, which is partly true, and Alka watches him swing between shutting down and still applying.

row_description: Accepts hugs, offers a kiss or a toy, and seeks the elder's lap; warmth is learned by being received.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: On the verandah of the village house, Dadi sat shelling peas while the afternoon bus rattled past. Naveen toddled over, dropped a small clay bullock in her lap and climbed up after it. She wrapped her arm around him and kissed his hair. He patted her cheek, then gave her a wet, loud kiss of his own. He stayed there, head on her shoulder, watching a hen cross the yard, and the peas waited.

qa.q: What was Dadi doing when Naveen came over?
qa.a: She was shelling peas on the verandah.

qa.q: What does Naveen want when he drops the clay bullock and climbs into Dadi's lap?
qa.a: He wants closeness and to share something he likes with her. His pat on her cheek and his kiss show that he feels warm and safe with her.

qa.q: What does Dadi's response teach Naveen?
qa.a: Her open arms and kiss show him that affection is welcome, so he learns to give it too.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Naveen kisses her?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and cherished, enough to let the peas wait. ❤️

record.grounding: A toddler accepts a grandmother's hug, offers a toy and a kiss, and seeks her lap in a village home.

row_description: The small one clutches the toy and screams, having no words for mine. Caregivers should step in gently, name the feeling, and offer another turn rather than forcing sharing at once.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage: In the flat's small living room, Sharmila clutched her doll to her chest and screamed. Her older sister Minakshi had reached for it. Mama came over quickly and crouched between them. "Sharmila is holding it tight. She's saying mine." She turned to Minakshi. "You can have a turn when Sharmila is finished. Here, take the teddy for now." Sharmila's screams dropped to hiccups, though she still kept a hand on the doll.

qa.q: What did Sharmila clutch to her chest?
qa.a: Sharmila clutched her doll.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling and wanting when she screamed?
qa.a: She wanted to keep the doll and protect it, and she had no words to say mine, so she screamed.

qa.q: What could Mama do next to help both girls?
qa.a: Name the feeling, promise Minakshi a turn later, offer her another toy and not force Sharmila to give up the doll at once.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Mama tells her to wait?
qa.a: She may feel a little left out or impatient, but being offered the teddy and a promised turn helps her know she is not forgotten.

record.grounding: Shows a small child clutching a toy and screaming when a sibling reaches for it, and a caregiver naming the feeling and offering another turn.

row_description: People in my temple, mosque or church go cold when I question things. I feel lonely. Wise: find one or two open-minded elders or peers, and value people over doctrine wins. Harmful: cutting all ties in anger.
recipe_text: An interview-style or spoken monologue: the protagonist tells the story aloud to a friend, podcast host or interviewer.

record.passage:
I'm Kunal, and the strangest part wasn't the questions, it was the silence after. I'd asked the temple committee why we do one ritual the way we do, and whether it had to be this way. Not to be rude. I wanted to know.

The next Sunday, aunties who used to press prasad into my hand looked past me. Talk stopped when I walked up. I stood by the shoe rack feeling like a stranger in a place I grew up in. Honestly, I was angry. I almost decided never to go back.

What changed things was Samir Uncle, who kept the temple library. He said, "Come, help me sort these books. Questions are fine here." And one friend from the youth group kept sitting next to me.

I don't agree with everyone there. But those two mattered more than any argument.

qa.q: Who kept the temple library?
qa.a: Samir Uncle kept the temple library.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel standing by the shoe rack?
qa.a: Kunal felt like a stranger in a place Kunal grew up in, lonely and angry enough to nearly decide never to go back.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Kunal to hold on to a couple of people?
qa.a: Samir Uncle and the friend welcomed questions, so Kunal did not have to cut every tie in anger and could keep the community through people, not doctrine.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Kunal's questions?
qa.a: The aunties may hear the questions as a challenge to something they love, so they go quiet, which could be discomfort rather than a plan to shun Kunal.

record.grounding: People in the temple go cold when Kunal questions, Kunal feels lonely, and finds one elder and one peer who stay open.

row_description: In games, older users offer gifts and free items for friendship. Wise: notice why an adult is giving gifts to a teen and never accept things that come with secrecy.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage:
I'm Sumit, and I was on the sofa while my cousin Mridul played online in our flat. He kept grinning at the screen. "An older player gave me a rare skin for free. He says I'm the best he's met, and I should add him on a private chat."
Then Mridul hesitated. "He also said not to tell my parents, because they'd make me stop." His grin dropped a little.
I asked, "Why would a grown-up give free stuff to a kid and want it kept secret?" He shrugged and said the skin was cool, but he didn't look sure.
Later I saw him remove the friend request. At dinner he told his mother. I don't know whether he was scared or just tired of it.

qa.q: What did the older player give Mridul for free?
qa.a: He gave Mridul a rare skin.

qa.q: What did Mridul seem to be feeling when he hesitated?
qa.a: His grin dropped a little and he didn't look sure, so he seemed uneasy about the gift and the secrecy, though Sumit can't know for certain.

qa.q: What could Mridul do when someone offers gifts that come with secrecy?
qa.a: He can refuse gifts that come with secrecy, remove the contact and tell his parents or another trusted adult, as he did at dinner.

qa.q: How did Sumit's question change the way Mridul saw the gift?
qa.a: Sumit asked why a grown-up would give a kid free things and want it kept secret, which made Mridul look at the gift from another angle.

record.grounding: Shows a teen offered gifts by an older gaming contact who asks for secrecy, and choosing to refuse and tell his mother.

row_description: I told my best friend a secret and now everyone knows. I feel hot and hurt. Wise: tell her how it felt and decide how much to trust her later. It is fine to be careful, but not to be cruel back.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative set outside India (any country), ordinary everyday detail.

record.passage: On the walk to the tram stop in Lisbon, Javier called out, "Night-light Rafael!" and two other boys laughed. Rafael's ears burned. Only Marisol knew he still slept with a small lamp on. He had told her in Year Five, and she had sworn on her bracelet. He said nothing all the way home, chewing his lip, and threw his bag on the bed hard. Next morning he found Marisol by the lockers. "You told," he said, voice low. "It felt awful, like everyone was looking inside my room." Marisol's face went red. He did not shout, and he did not spread her secrets. He only said he needed some time before telling her anything else.

qa.q: What did Javier call out to Rafael?
qa.a: Javier called out "Night-light Rafael!"

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he stayed silent on the way home, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hurt and hot with embarrassment: his ears burned, he chewed his lip and threw his bag on the bed hard.

qa.q: What would you advise Rafael about trusting Marisol from now on?
qa.a: It is fine to be careful and share only small things for a while, but not to get back at her by spreading her secrets.

qa.q: What might Marisol be feeling when Rafael says "You told"?
qa.a: Her face went red, so she is probably ashamed and worried, and she may want to explain or say sorry.

record.grounding: A child's secret told to a best friend is now known by everyone; he feels hot and hurt, says how it felt, and becomes careful without being cruel back.
